sections.section_title: Testing the Spirits -- The Criterion of the Incarnation
sections.summary: The neutral reading found that the community must test spirits by whether they confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh: the spirit that confesses this is from God, while the spirit that does not confess Jesus is the spirit of the antichrist, already present in the world.

sections.section_title: Two Origins, Two Audiences -- The Community's Victory Over the False Prophets
sections.summary: The neutral reading found that the community has already overcome the false prophets because 'greater is He who is in you than he who is in the world,' and that two diagnostic criteria distinguish the spirit of truth from the spirit of error: reception of the apostolic message and alignment with the christological confession.
sections.relevance: The passage provides strong language of accomplished victory: the community 'has overcome them' (perfect tense, indicating completed action with ongoing results). The basis of the victory is not the community's own strength but the superior power of the one who indwells them (the Spirit of God). This supports the permanence view by emphasizing that the community's security rests on divine power rather than human performance. However, the passage is specifically about the community's victory over the false prophets' theological influence, not a universal guarantee against all forms of spiritual failure.
key_phrases: you are from God, little children, and have overcome them
greater is He who is in you than he who is in the world
by this we know the spirit of truth and the spirit of error

sections.section_title: Love, the Nature of God, and the Incarnation as Love's Supreme Expression
sections.summary: The neutral reading found that love originates from God, that everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God, that the one who does not love does not know God because God is love, that God demonstrated his love by sending his Son as propitiation for sins, and that God's love is perfected in the community when they love one another.
sections.relevance: The passage establishes love as the criterion for whether a person truly knows God: 'The one who does not love does not know God, because God is love.' The aorist tense (ouk egno, 'never knew') suggests that the non-lover never arrived at genuine knowledge of God. This could support either reading: permanence (the non-lover was never genuine) or conditionality (failure to love disqualifies the claim to know God). The passage also states that God's love reaches its intended completion (is 'perfected') only when the community practices mutual love, implying that the love-circuit is not automatic but requires active participation. The invisible God is made present through mutual love; its absence leaves the community without the evidence of God's dwelling among them.
key_phrases: everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God
the one who does not love does not know God, because God is love
if we love one another, God remains in us, and His love is perfected in us

sections.section_title: The Spirit, the Eyewitness Testimony, and Confession as the Basis of Mutual Indwelling
sections.summary: The neutral reading found that the Spirit given by God is the evidence of mutual indwelling, that the eyewitness community testifies that the Father sent the Son as Savior of the world, that confessing Jesus as the Son of God produces mutual indwelling with God, and that the community has come to know and believe the love God has for them.
sections.relevance: The passage provides multiple foundations for assurance of the believer's standing. The Spirit, described as a completed gift (perfect tense dedoken, 'has given'), is the permanent evidence of mutual indwelling. The community's knowledge and belief in God's love are described with perfect tenses (egnokamen, pepisteukamen) indicating settled, ongoing states. The confession that 'Jesus is the Son of God' produces mutual indwelling ('God remains in him, and he in God'). These elements support permanence: what God has given (the Spirit) and what the community has come to know (God's love) are presented as settled realities. However, the confession and the indwelling are described in relational terms that imply ongoing engagement rather than a static transaction.
key_phrases: He has given to us of His Spirit
the Father has sent the Son to be the Savior of the world
whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him, and he in God
we have come to know and have believed the love which God has for us

sections.section_title: God Is Love, Mutual Indwelling, and Confidence in the Day of Judgment
sections.summary: The neutral reading found that the one who remains in love remains in God and God in him, that love is perfected so the community may have confidence in the day of judgment, and that perfect love drives out fear because fear is oriented toward punishment.
sections.relevance: The passage provides a strong basis for the believer's assurance: perfected love produces confidence on the day of judgment, and perfect love 'drives out fear' (ekballo, the same verb used for casting out demons -- love forcefully ejects fear). The correspondence 'as He is, we also are in this world' grounds the confidence in the community's present likeness to Christ in love. This supports permanence by connecting the community's standing at judgment to their present participation in God's love. However, the passage also implies that love must be 'perfected' -- brought to its goal -- and that 'the one who fears is not perfected in love,' suggesting a process that can be incomplete rather than an automatic guarantee.
key_phrases: the one who remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him
love is perfected with us, so that we may have confidence in the day of judgment
there is no fear in love, but perfect love drives out fear

sections.section_title: The Source of Our Love and the Inseparability of Love for God and Love for the Brother
sections.summary: The neutral reading found that the community loves because God first loved them, that claiming to love God while hating a brother makes one a liar, that the one who cannot love the visible brother cannot love the invisible God, and that the commandment binds love for God and love for the brother together as inseparable.
sections.relevance: The passage continues the letter's diagnostic method of testing verbal claims against conduct. The claim 'I love God' is falsified by hatred of a brother. The inability (ou dynatai, 'cannot') to love the invisible God while hating the visible brother is stated as a logical and spiritual impossibility. This bears on the question because it establishes that love for God -- the defining mark of relationship with God -- is inseparable from love for fellow believers. A person who claims relationship with God but fails to love the community is declared a 'liar.' The passage implies that the believer's standing is verified or falsified by the presence or absence of love for the community.
key_phrases: we love, because He first loved us
if someone says I love God and yet he hates his brother, he is a liar
the one who does not love his brother whom he has seen, cannot love God whom he has not seen
